description: A very heavy, fine-textured hardwood whose heartwood is close to jet black. Prized for small, high-value parts such as instrument fingerboards and fittings, knife and tool handles, inlay, and turned details.

hazards.summary: Occupational asthma from ebony dust has been confirmed by inhalation challenge, once in a worker exposed to Diospyros crassiflora and once in a violin maker sanding ebony fingerboards. Skin testing was negative in the first case, so the mechanism is not known.
The UK HSE lists ebony as a cause of dermatitis and as a possible skin sensitiser. Its listing covers ebony in general rather than naming a particular Diospyros species.
HSE also lists irritation of the moist linings of the nose, throat and eyes among the reported effects of ebony dust.
IARC classifies all wood dust as carcinogenic to humans, chiefly through cancers of the nose and sinuses. This applies to African ebony dust as it does to any other wood.

image_prompt: Photorealistic studio photograph of a freshly planed African ebony (Diospyros crassiflora) board, shot at a low three-quarter angle so the face grain fills most of the frame. Dense, uniform jet-black heartwood with occasional faint dark-brown streaks, and no visible sapwood. Very fine, even texture with tiny closed pores, nearly invisible straight grain, and a soft satin sheen where the light catches the surface. Soft diffused daylight from upper left, gentle falloff, neutral warm-grey seamless background, shallow depth of field with the near edge tack-sharp. No text, no logos, no hands, no tools, no finish or varnish, natural unfinished wood. Wide 1200x630 composition (1.91:1) with the board centered and margin on both sides for cropping.
image_alt: Planed board of African ebony with dense, nearly uniform jet-black heartwood and a subtle satin sheen.
notes_internal: Maestrelli-1987 is the only reviewed primary paper that names D. crassiflora; KopferschmittKubler-1992 abstract says only 'ebony'. HSE-WIS30 'Ebony' is not species-specific. Ebony skin case reports (Wlodek 2014, Kuner 2004, Rouyer 2026) found but not cited because species and test details could not be confirmed from abstracts; see data/verify/african-tropicals.md. 'Gaboon ebony' is a trade name for this wood; do not confuse with gaboon/okoume (slug okoume).
